item.title: The Daily Star – Beyond microcredit: What Bangladesh’s poor really need
item.description:
Jonathan Morduch, professor of public policy and economics at New York University's Wagner Graduate School of Public Service and co-author of Portfolios of the Poor, has studied how low-income households in Bangladesh manage their finances since the early 1990s. In an interview with The Daily Star, he reflects on nearly five decades of microfinance in Bangladesh, its achievements and limitations, the transformative role of migration, remittances and the garment industry in reducing poverty, and why the next chapter of financial inclusion must focus on savings, flexibility and consumer protection.

The Daily Star (TDS): Bangladesh has nearly five decades of experience with microfinance. Looking back, what has microfinance actually achieved, and how does that differ from what it originally promised?

Jonathan Morduch (JM): It is actually a complicated question. Microcredit began with a very strong promise and a very strong narrative, built around a story that Muhammad Yunus told many times about working with a small group in a village outside his university in Chittagong. It highlighted the possibility that even poor people could borrow money, repay it and have entrepreneurial ambitions.
Professor Jonathan Morduch

That narrative was very successful in selling Grameen, both within Bangladesh and outside it. Donors were looking for ways to help reduce poverty, but they worried that if they just gave money to poor people, it would be wasted, used inefficiently or corruptly, or worse. Yunus's narrative pushed back against that. It was very clever because the fact that the money was going to women and that they were paying it back suggested they were doing something meaningful with it. Some people call it “the market test”. It has been criticised, but it was a very powerful piece of logic.

I think it was also problematic. To judge the success or failure of microcredit, you have to look not at how it was sold internationally and domestically, but at what it really did. When researchers asked borrowers what they were really doing with the money they borrowed, they often replied that they had used the loan to pay school fees, to buy grain for the coming season, to save a little or to pay off a different loan. Maybe half the time or more, these were not business activities.

So, in a real sense, the great contribution of microcredit was to provide liquidity: to bring money to people who were struggling just to manage their finances and meet their basic needs in a very unstable environment. That is a more complicated message to sell, internationally or even domestically, but it is truer to how people use microfinance. In that sense, we wouldn't expect microfinance to revolutionise or transform people's lives, but it could still make a difference.

One more thing is often missed in evaluations of whether microfinance worked or not: microcredit was a remarkable achievement in creating a reliable institution in villages that were not well served. The staff would show up at the right time with the right amount of money. They would promise a loan, deliver that loan, and people could count on it. At a time when electricity and many other services were not particularly reliable, that level of reliability was no small thing. And once that structure was built, BRAC and others could start layering other services onto it.

So, looking back, microcredit had many successes that would have been hard to imagine beforehand. I just don't think they were the successes that were popularised internationally.

TDS: Why has microfinance not delivered the entrepreneurial transformation it originally promised, despite reaching millions of people?

JM: Because I think most people were not looking for that kind of transformation. Yunus, I think, still strongly believes that everyone can be an entrepreneur. He himself is a brilliant entrepreneur and institution builder. But a lot of people don't want to start their own businesses. It's difficult, and they don't share the kind of ambition that he himself exhibits.

One reason microcredit was transformative is that customers were looking for a different kind of service, and they found it in microcredit. The promise was misaligned with what customers actually wanted. But that doesn't make it a failure. It makes it a different kind of proposition.
A woman trained by a local NGO makes dolls using jute and other plant fibres to earn a living. Microcredit can help small-scale producers invest when economic opportunities arise. Photo: Prabir Das

People can use microcredit for lots of things, and part of the answer lies in the structure of microcredit lending. Whether it is Grameen, BRAC or ASA, the structure is very similar: you borrow an amount of money and repay it in small instalments. In many ways, it was a stroke of genius to do it that way, because people can repay very easily in small sums rather than in one large sum at the end.

On the other hand, it is a very strange way to make a business loan. Usually, a business owner would borrow money, go away for a few months, develop their business, earn some profit and repay the loan at the end of, say, six months. If instead I said, “Look, I'm going to give you this loan, and I need you to start repaying it next week”, you might accept it if that were the only kind of loan you could get. But it is a really strange system for what is described as a business loan.

What the structure did, though (and I don't think this story is well told), was allow people to borrow for many purposes. That instalment pattern looks like a consumer loan, not a producer loan. When I make a purchase on my credit card, I repay it month by month; that is how a lot of consumer finance works. That structure allowed people to feel comfortable borrowing to buy food, to buy medicine and to do many things that simply helped them manage their lives better, knowing they could repay in instalments.
Workers sew clothes on the production floor of a garment factory in Bangladesh. The garment industry and remittances have played a transformative role in improving the livelihoods of low-income households. Photo: Sourav Hossain Siam

The second thing the structure did was allow people to repay not from the profits of a business but from the income coming into the household. The son has some work, the daughter has some work, the husband has some work. There are regular flows of income, and those flows can go towards repaying the loan.

So, are these outcomes systemic? It was not inevitable that people would use microfinance for all kinds of purposes, but when you look closely at what actually happens, the design enables it. In fact, it is well designed for it. That story is often hidden. But it works for the microlenders because it gives them a much bigger customer base. And it is often exactly what customers want and need.

TDS: Your research suggests that conventional poverty measures can overlook periods of deprivation within a year. How should this understanding inform the design of microfinance products and the assessment of their impact?

JM: The year-long microcredit loan with instalments is well designed for lots of purposes, but not for situations characterised by crises and recurrent risks. It is quite structured. That is an advantage most of the time, but in a crisis, it offers very little flexibility. People then need to borrow from another source to repay the loan. That can be a real problem with microcredit.

So one answer is to design financial products with more flexibility built in. There is research showing that when people have access to a product that lets them skip a few instalments and pay later, they actually do better. They invest more, and the product better fits their needs.

More broadly, that part of my work was inspired by the fact that many studies look at outcomes before and after and say, “Look, microcredit was not transformative; it didn't change poverty.” But that is partly because poverty is usually measured by average annual consumption. Microcredit may actually have been helping people reduce their exposure to poverty during the year, even if their average consumption did not rise. This is because it lets people save more easily or borrow ahead of a coming lean season. In that way, it can address poverty by helping people protect themselves in difficult times. I think that could be encouraged rather than hidden behind the narrative of transformation.

TDS: How have migration, remittances and the garment industry transformed rural Bangladesh, and what role has microfinance played in that transformation?

JM: I think the real transformation may come from a different direction. Microcredit and similar interventions started with the logic that rural poverty should be addressed by putting more resources directly into rural areas. But many rural workers themselves said: actually, I want to leave home and find a job in the city, where there are steadier and better-paying jobs. So, from the household's perspective, the question is not just how to increase earnings in villages. It is how a household can increase its resources through a range of strategies, which can involve migration, with remittances then sent back home.

For a long time, a big story in villages has been remittances, not just from abroad but also from within Bangladesh. That can be much more transformative than anything else going on. But something else has happened too. As the ready-made garment (RMG) sector grew, the government had more resources and became more ambitious, and you started to see roads and other infrastructure being built. That in itself creates and strengthens markets, which in turn creates jobs. The construction of roads, new government buildings and other offices also creates jobs for both men and women.
Migrant workers wait at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka following flight cancellations and delays. Despite their transformative contribution to Bangladesh’s economy through remittances, migrant workers often face considerable hardship and remain insufficiently recognised. Photo: Anisur Rahman

The remittance revolution in Bangladesh and the RMG sector have both been fairly pro-poor, surprisingly. That could not be taken for granted, and I think it is what has really transformed areas that were extremely poor before. It is not just the direct impacts but also the spillover effects: they generate more economic activity, more tax revenue and other kinds of investment, and the effects build over time. Microcredit, in that context, helps people manage these changes and take advantage of them: to migrate more easily or to invest a bit more when an opportunity arises. But it is not driving these processes. It is helping people tap into them.

TDS: What should Bangladesh prioritise to make economic growth more inclusive and reduce poverty?

JM: If you look at the data across countries, the biggest driver of poverty reduction has been economic growth. We see this in China, in India and in Bangladesh. But even if the data show the importance of growth very clearly, it is not so simple. You don't just flip a switch and growth happens. So-called “inclusive growth” is even harder.

One way to think about the economic transformations in Bangladesh is to imagine an engine that is creating jobs and opportunities, together with institutions like microfinance that help people take steps on their own: to migrate, to send remittances back home and to take up jobs in cities. Then, as jobs and growth build, those institutions help people tap into that process more effectively and cope with the risks it creates. That requires financial tools, not to build a business, but perhaps to build up enough savings for a family member to move to Dhaka and take advantage of the new economy.

That cannot be taken for granted. You need growth, but you also need a way for a broad group of people to take advantage of it. Otherwise, growth happens and only richer people benefit, or growth itself may not gain momentum. In many ways, it is low-income Bangladeshis who have driven this period of growth. They provided the labour that generated the remittances and helped build the RMG sector. I think the country really owes a debt to people who have been working very, very hard for their own sake, often in difficult conditions, and in the process have been building the country.
One of microcredit’s most significant achievements in Bangladesh has been the establishment of reliable financial institutions in rural communities that were previously underserved. Illustration: Salman Sakib Shahryar

TDS: What financial services and protections should Bangladesh prioritise to better serve low-income households?

JM: I have two priorities. The first is savings. We are already seeing the use of microcredit decline, especially after the pandemic, because people are asking: Why am I paying all this money to borrow when I could be saving on my own? So helping people save is a natural step beyond credit. In the beginning, when Yunus and others started, saving just wasn't seen as interesting or possible. But as we have come to understand what people's lives are really like, we have seen that people do want to save, and they can save. They need to save and borrow at the same time, and the mix now seems to be shifting more towards saving.

The second is consumer protection of all kinds, but especially in digital finance. I have just been in villages in the north, and everyone has a story of a scam that directly affected them or a close relative. It is keeping people from using these services, and it creates a lot of uncertainty. It may be their last Tk 2,000 or Tk 10,000, sometimes more. If you are well off, that may not be much money. But if you are struggling in a village, it can be a lot of money to lose, with no means of getting it back.

So protections and regulations that ensure accountability on the part of providers, make it easier to seek redress and help people know where to turn when problems arise are all very important steps.

The interview was conducted by Khairul Hassan Jahin and Musrat Hossain Mithila.

item.title: The Daily Star – Afterlife of political power: Children of Bangladesh’s fallen establishment
item.description:
Political upheaval does not end when a government falls. For the children of those who once occupied positions of influence, its consequences can follow them across borders, into universities, relationships and the consulting room.

As a psychiatrist working in Australia, including with people from migrant and diaspora communities, I have increasingly encountered young Bangladeshis whose personal circumstances have been shaped by the political upheaval of recent years. Some are international students. Their immediate concerns may appear familiar: relationships, anxiety, substance use, identity and the challenges of establishing themselves in a new country. Yet behind these ordinary difficulties can lie an unusually complicated family history.

When Sheikh Hasina’s government collapsed in August 2024, it marked the end of more than a decade of political dominance. Hasina fled to India in the wake of student-led protests and the violent confrontations that followed. The consequences have extended well beyond Bangladesh. Families associated with the former administration have dispersed across the world. Some have sought refuge in neighbouring countries, while others have established themselves in Britain, Australia, Canada and elsewhere. For some, this movement represents political survival; for others, it may involve the preservation of wealth, educational opportunities and family security following a dramatic loss of influence.

The following portraits, using pseudonyms and deliberately altered or blended details, illustrate some of the themes I have encountered. They are not intended as identifiable clinical case histories.

Consider Janak, a young international student whose family was once associated with a prominent political establishment in Bangladesh. His parents have now left the country and are living elsewhere in the region. He is preoccupied with questions of status and family reputation. There is a sense that the family has experienced a humiliating reversal of fortune: people who once occupied positions of influence are now dispersed, anxious about their future and separated from the country in which their standing was established.
Children may find themselves managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves. Photo: Collected/Unsplash

Janak has another problem. He has developed a significant dependence on cannabis but finds it almost impossible to acknowledge that he has an addiction. The word itself seems to represent an intolerable loss of status. In his understanding, addiction is associated with personal failure, weakness and social disgrace. His reluctance to accept the terminology makes it difficult to engage him in treatment.

This is not simply a case of an individual resisting a psychiatric label. In many South Asian communities, mental illness and substance dependence carry considerable stigma. Family reputation, educational achievement and the appearance of personal success are particularly important. Acknowledging a drug problem may feel like admitting a failure that extends beyond the individual to the family.

Janak’s predicament suggests a collision between two threatened identities: the loss of inherited family status and the fear of acquiring a new, stigmatised personal identity. The young man who cannot bear to be regarded as an addict may also be struggling to understand what remains of the identity his family once provided.

A second young person, whom I will call Shapna, presents a different dilemma. She is studying at a Sydney university and has established a social circle, largely among other Bangladeshis. She has a social media presence that connects her to people back home and has spent time living in different countries. Her father, a senior figure associated with the former political establishment, appears to have considerable wealth, the origins of which she does not fully understand.

Shapna seems conscious that her family’s financial circumstances are not straightforward. She has suspicions about the origins of some of her father’s money, but she also benefits from the family’s resources. She feels sympathy for her parents, who have been displaced from Bangladesh, and wants to support them. There is no simple way for her to separate affection for her family from questions about the legitimacy of its wealth.

This is an uncomfortable moral position, although not an unusual one in families where wealth and political influence have been intertwined. Children are rarely responsible for the circumstances in which their parents accumulated their fortunes. Nor should they automatically be expected to reject the material benefits of family life. But they may find themselves living with an uneasy awareness that the advantages they enjoy could have been acquired through improper means.
Protesters gather at Ganabhaban, the prime minister’s official residence in Dhaka, following the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government on 5 August 2024. The consequences of this loss of political power extend well beyond Bangladesh. Photo: AFP

There is a useful international parallel here. In a 2021 report for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, researcher Matthew Page examined the overseas education of children of politically exposed persons from West Africa, particularly Nigeria and Ghana. He identified at least 100 children of politically exposed persons who were attending or had recently attended British educational institutions. The report raised concerns that some tuition payments might involve unexplained or illicit wealth. It also explored how elite families use international education to reproduce social status, establish networks and protect their children’s futures.

This is relevant to Bangladesh. Our universities and financial institutions are not the only places where the consequences of political patronage can be felt. The international education system, property markets and financial networks can all become destinations for wealth accumulated in circumstances that deserve scrutiny. This is not an accusation against individual students but a broader question about the relationship between international mobility, family privilege and the preservation of wealth.

A third experience involves a Bangladeshi-Australian woman, whom I will call Mira. She married a man she had met during her university studies without initially appreciating the extent of his family’s political connections. Only later did she discover that he was closely associated with a prominent political family. Following the political upheaval in Bangladesh, her husband has gone into hiding in Dhaka, fearing for his safety. She remains in Sydney with their young child.

She has expressed sympathy for the former government, arguing that the extent of its corruption has been exaggerated and expressing enthusiasm about the possibility of Sheikh Hasina returning to Bangladesh. She also draws comparisons with Australian politics, pointing to scandals and questionable conduct among Australian politicians. There is perhaps an understandable instinct to temper accusations against one’s own family by pointing to the imperfections of other political systems.

These experiences invite a broader consideration of what might be called the psychological afterlife of political power. The fall of a government may be a discrete historical event, but for families associated with it, the consequences can persist for years. The loss of status, uncertainty surrounding wealth, fear of political retribution and the need to reconstruct identity do not disappear when someone crosses an international border.

The sociologist Arlie Hochschild’s concept of emotion work offers one way of understanding this process. In a 2025 study in the Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, Verónica Díaz Cerda examined the experiences of children of Chilean political exiles, including those born in Britain to parents who had fled the Pinochet dictatorship. She described how children sometimes suppressed or evoked particular emotions to maintain a semblance of normality within families whose lives had been fractured by exile. They became agents of care, attempting to repair the emotional world of their parents, sometimes at the cost of their own emotional well-being. Although the circumstances of Chilean political refugees differ substantially from those of the children of Bangladesh’s former ruling establishment, the idea of emotion work is illuminating. Children can become responsible for managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves.
For children of former political elites, the ordinary demands of young adulthood may be compounded by a parent’s loss of power, uncertainty surrounding family wealth or a political history that is difficult to discuss.

There is a further historical dimension in Bangladesh. The country’s 1971 Liberation War remains a powerful part of the identity of many families. For some parents who participated in or were deeply affected by the liberation struggle, the events of that period have never entirely receded into history. Their children may inherit not simply stories of national independence but also the emotional and political loyalties associated with it. In some families, political identity is transmitted almost as a form of inheritance. The events of 2024, however, have created a new rupture, involving a younger generation whose experience of Bangladesh may increasingly be shaped by displacement and distance.

Even the Bangladeshi diaspora in the West has felt the repercussions. Tulip Siddiq, the British Labour MP and niece of Sheikh Hasina, resigned as a Treasury minister in January 2025 after questions arose about London properties associated with members of her family and people connected to the former Bangladeshi government. She maintained that she had done nothing wrong. The episode nevertheless illustrated how the political history of Bangladesh could reach into the professional and public lives of people who had built careers abroad.

The future remains uncertain. Hasina has continued to indicate that she intends to return to Bangladesh. In an interview with the Associated Press in November 2026, she reiterated her intention to return in December, despite having been sentenced to death in absentia in 2025 over the crackdown on protesters. She disputes the verdict and the legitimacy of the proceedings. Whether she returns or not, the possibility itself has significance for families divided between Bangladesh and their new countries of residence. It keeps alive the sense that the political story is not finished and that the fortunes of those associated with the former government may change again.

These circumstances offer a reminder that mental health cannot always be understood solely in terms of an individual’s immediate circumstances. Anxiety, addiction, depression and difficulties with identity may be connected to a family history that is politically complicated, morally ambiguous and sometimes deliberately concealed. The patient sitting in front of us may be negotiating not only the ordinary demands of young adulthood but also the emotional consequences of a parent’s loss of power, a family’s uncertain wealth or a political history that is difficult to discuss.

Perhaps the most interesting feature of this generation is the tension between inherited privilege and inherited uncertainty. The children of political elites may retain their education, wealth and international connections but lose the certainty that once accompanied their family name. They must negotiate a new identity in countries that offer freedom and opportunity while carrying the unresolved history of a political establishment whose fate remains contested.

Political power is usually studied through the actions of leaders, institutions and movements. Its aftermath deserves to be examined through the experiences of families who inherit its consequences. The fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government was a defining moment in Bangladesh’s modern history. For some younger members of the Bangladeshi diaspora, however, the event is not simply something that happened in their country of origin. It is something they continue to live with, in their relationships, their identities and sometimes in the consulting room.

Political upheaval does not end when a government falls. For the children of those who once occupied positions of influence, its consequences can follow them across borders, into universities, relationships and the consulting room.

As a psychiatrist working in Australia, including with people from migrant and diaspora communities, I have increasingly encountered young Bangladeshis whose personal circumstances have been shaped by the political upheaval of recent years. Some are international students. Their immediate concerns may appear familiar: relationships, anxiety, substance use, identity and the challenges of establishing themselves in a new country. Yet behind these ordinary difficulties can lie an unusually complicated family history.

When Sheikh Hasina’s government collapsed in August 2024, it marked the end of more than a decade of political dominance. Hasina fled to India in the wake of student-led protests and the violent confrontations that followed. The consequences have extended well beyond Bangladesh. Families associated with the former administration have dispersed across the world. Some have sought refuge in neighbouring countries, while others have established themselves in Britain, Australia, Canada and elsewhere. For some, this movement represents political survival; for others, it may involve the preservation of wealth, educational opportunities and family security following a dramatic loss of influence.

The following portraits, using pseudonyms and deliberately altered or blended details, illustrate some of the themes I have encountered. They are not intended as identifiable clinical case histories.

Consider Janak, a young international student whose family was once associated with a prominent political establishment in Bangladesh. His parents have now left the country and are living elsewhere in the region. He is preoccupied with questions of status and family reputation. There is a sense that the family has experienced a humiliating reversal of fortune: people who once occupied positions of influence are now dispersed, anxious about their future and separated from the country in which their standing was established.
Children may find themselves managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves. Photo: Collected/Unsplash

Janak has another problem. He has developed a significant dependence on cannabis but finds it almost impossible to acknowledge that he has an addiction. The word itself seems to represent an intolerable loss of status. In his understanding, addiction is associated with personal failure, weakness and social disgrace. His reluctance to accept the terminology makes it difficult to engage him in treatment.

This is not simply a case of an individual resisting a psychiatric label. In many South Asian communities, mental illness and substance dependence carry considerable stigma. Family reputation, educational achievement and the appearance of personal success are particularly important. Acknowledging a drug problem may feel like admitting a failure that extends beyond the individual to the family.

Janak’s predicament suggests a collision between two threatened identities: the loss of inherited family status and the fear of acquiring a new, stigmatised personal identity. The young man who cannot bear to be regarded as an addict may also be struggling to understand what remains of the identity his family once provided.

A second young person, whom I will call Shapna, presents a different dilemma. She is studying at a Sydney university and has established a social circle, largely among other Bangladeshis. She has a social media presence that connects her to people back home and has spent time living in different countries. Her father, a senior figure associated with the former political establishment, appears to have considerable wealth, the origins of which she does not fully understand.

Shapna seems conscious that her family’s financial circumstances are not straightforward. She has suspicions about the origins of some of her father’s money, but she also benefits from the family’s resources. She feels sympathy for her parents, who have been displaced from Bangladesh, and wants to support them. There is no simple way for her to separate affection for her family from questions about the legitimacy of its wealth.

This is an uncomfortable moral position, although not an unusual one in families where wealth and political influence have been intertwined. Children are rarely responsible for the circumstances in which their parents accumulated their fortunes. Nor should they automatically be expected to reject the material benefits of family life. But they may find themselves living with an uneasy awareness that the advantages they enjoy could have been acquired through improper means.
Protesters gather at Ganabhaban, the prime minister’s official residence in Dhaka, following the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government on 5 August 2024. The consequences of this loss of political power extend well beyond Bangladesh. Photo: AFP

There is a useful international parallel here. In a 2021 report for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, researcher Matthew Page examined the overseas education of children of politically exposed persons from West Africa, particularly Nigeria and Ghana. He identified at least 100 children of politically exposed persons who were attending or had recently attended British educational institutions. The report raised concerns that some tuition payments might involve unexplained or illicit wealth. It also explored how elite families use international education to reproduce social status, establish networks and protect their children’s futures.

This is relevant to Bangladesh. Our universities and financial institutions are not the only places where the consequences of political patronage can be felt. The international education system, property markets and financial networks can all become destinations for wealth accumulated in circumstances that deserve scrutiny. This is not an accusation against individual students but a broader question about the relationship between international mobility, family privilege and the preservation of wealth.

A third experience involves a Bangladeshi-Australian woman, whom I will call Mira. She married a man she had met during her university studies without initially appreciating the extent of his family’s political connections. Only later did she discover that he was closely associated with a prominent political family. Following the political upheaval in Bangladesh, her husband has gone into hiding in Dhaka, fearing for his safety. She remains in Sydney with their young child.

She has expressed sympathy for the former government, arguing that the extent of its corruption has been exaggerated and expressing enthusiasm about the possibility of Sheikh Hasina returning to Bangladesh. She also draws comparisons with Australian politics, pointing to scandals and questionable conduct among Australian politicians. There is perhaps an understandable instinct to temper accusations against one’s own family by pointing to the imperfections of other political systems.

These experiences invite a broader consideration of what might be called the psychological afterlife of political power. The fall of a government may be a discrete historical event, but for families associated with it, the consequences can persist for years. The loss of status, uncertainty surrounding wealth, fear of political retribution and the need to reconstruct identity do not disappear when someone crosses an international border.

The sociologist Arlie Hochschild’s concept of emotion work offers one way of understanding this process. In a 2025 study in the Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, Verónica Díaz Cerda examined the experiences of children of Chilean political exiles, including those born in Britain to parents who had fled the Pinochet dictatorship. She described how children sometimes suppressed or evoked particular emotions to maintain a semblance of normality within families whose lives had been fractured by exile. They became agents of care, attempting to repair the emotional world of their parents, sometimes at the cost of their own emotional well-being. Although the circumstances of Chilean political refugees differ substantially from those of the children of Bangladesh’s former ruling establishment, the idea of emotion work is illuminating. Children can become responsible for managing the emotional consequences of their parents’ political experiences, even when they have little control over the events themselves.
For children of former political elites, the ordinary demands of young adulthood may be compounded by a parent’s loss of power, uncertainty surrounding family wealth or a political history that is difficult to discuss.

There is a further historical dimension in Bangladesh. The country’s 1971 Liberation War remains a powerful part of the identity of many families. For some parents who participated in or were deeply affected by the liberation struggle, the events of that period have never entirely receded into history. Their children may inherit not simply stories of national independence but also the emotional and political loyalties associated with it. In some families, political identity is transmitted almost as a form of inheritance. The events of 2024, however, have created a new rupture, involving a younger generation whose experience of Bangladesh may increasingly be shaped by displacement and distance.

Even the Bangladeshi diaspora in the West has felt the repercussions. Tulip Siddiq, the British Labour MP and niece of Sheikh Hasina, resigned as a Treasury minister in January 2025 after questions arose about London properties associated with members of her family and people connected to the former Bangladeshi government. She maintained that she had done nothing wrong. item.title: The Daily Star – COP31 turns into CON31 : Climate diplomacy, fossil fuel politics and the theatre of global consensus
item.description:
The failure of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which concluded in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 22, 2026, to secure an overarching agreement exposed once again the widening chasm between the international community's recognition of the climate emergency and its capacity—and political willingness—to respond collectively. After more than two weeks of negotiations, extended beyond their scheduled conclusion, governments failed to agree on an overarching political declaration. The immediate disagreement concerned the omission of any explicit reference to fossil fuels and a pathway for transitioning away from coal, oil, and natural gas. Yet the failure was about considerably more than the wording of a diplomatic document. It revealed the unresolved political and economic contradictions at the heart of international climate governance: governments acknowledge the urgency of decarbonisation while remaining constrained by, and frequently invested in, the very energy systems that sustain global emissions. The question, therefore, is not simply why COP31 failed to reach consensus, but what the recurring inability to translate climate commitments into transformative action tells us about the institutional architecture of global climate diplomacy.

Thirty-one conferences into the process, the annual gathering of governments, diplomats, scientists, corporate representatives, environmental organisations, and civil society has grown into an immense machinery of international negotiation, but its elaborate institutional architecture has done little to overcome the political impasse at the heart of global climate action. The proliferation of these forums reflects a growing recognition that climate change transcends national boundaries and demands coordinated international responses. Yet the multiplication of conferences, declarations, pledges, and implementation frameworks has not produced a commensurate transformation of the global political economy. The gap between diplomatic ambition and material outcomes remains considerable. The irony is difficult to overlook: even as scientific evidence of accelerating climatic disruption becomes increasingly compelling, the negotiations intended to address it remain entangled in competing claims over energy security, economic competitiveness, national sovereignty, historical responsibility, and the distribution of financial burdens.

The question embedded in the title, COP31 Turns into CON31, is deliberately provocative. It asks whether the annual climate conference remains an effective instrument of collective action or has increasingly become a ritual through which governments perform environmental responsibility without having to undertake the political and economic transformations necessary to fulfil their commitments. The distinction is important. To characterize the entire COP process as a con would be to dismiss the genuine achievements of multilateral climate cooperation, not least the Paris Agreement. Yet to regard the continuation of diplomatic negotiations as evidence of meaningful progress would be equally misleading. The more consequential question is whether this institutional process has developed the political capacity to overcome the structural contradictions that repeatedly prevent its declarations and commitments from translating into substantive action.

The Ritual of Climate Diplomacy

The origins of contemporary climate negotiations lie in the 1992 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which established the principle that climate change required an internationally coordinated response. The annual conferences of the parties subsequently became the principal forum for negotiating commitments, reviewing progress, and developing mechanisms for cooperation. The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 introduced legally binding emissions-reduction targets for developed countries, although its limited participation and uneven implementation exposed the difficulties of reconciling international obligations with national economic interests.

The Paris Agreement of 2015 represented a significant change in approach. Rather than imposing a uniform system of emissions-reduction obligations, it established a framework under which countries would submit nationally determined contributions, periodically strengthen their ambitions, and participate in a collective process of reviewing progress. Its significance lay partly in the recognition that climate action required participation across developed and developing economies. The Paris Agreement established the collective objective of limiting the rise in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while committing its parties to pursuing efforts to restrict the increase to 1.5°C. 

The Paris framework was an important diplomatic achievement. It brought almost the entire international community into a common institutional arrangement and created a mechanism through which national commitments could be progressively strengthened. Yet its architecture also contained a fundamental limitation. The nationally determined character of the commitments preserved considerable discretion for governments, while its transparency and review mechanisms could expose inadequate performance without necessarily compelling corrective action. International cooperation was institutionalised, but the enforcement of national ambition remained limited.

This distinction between agreement and implementation has become central to the COP process. Governments can endorse ambitious temperature targets without agreeing on the domestic measures required to achieve them. They can acknowledge the need for a transition away from fossil fuels while continuing to subsidise, extract, export, and consume them. They can announce financial commitments without establishing sufficiently reliable mechanisms for delivering the resources that vulnerable countries require.

The resulting process is not necessarily fraudulent, nor should the achievements of multilateral climate cooperation be dismissed. Yet institutional legitimacy cannot be equated with substantive effectiveness. International negotiations inevitably involve competing interests, divergent development trajectories, and legitimate disagreements over historical responsibility, economic capacity, and the distribution of adjustment costs. These differences cannot simply be negotiated away. Nevertheless, the repeated production of ambitious declarations without commensurate implementation exposes a fundamental limitation of the process: diplomatic agreement does not necessarily translate into material transformation. A conference may succeed procedurally while leaving the political-economic structures responsible for continued dependence on fossil fuels and unequal exposure to climate risks largely intact. If successive conferences fail to confront these structural contradictions, the question will inevitably arise whether COP32 represents another step towards meaningful collective action or another iteration of COP turning into CON.
COP31 President Murat Kurum (third from left) joins former COP presidents and COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen (fourth from left) in a show of diplomatic unity in Antalya, Türkiye, on 10 November 2026, before negotiations stalled over fossil fuels and climate finance. Photo: Reuters

The Fossil-Fuel Contradiction

The failure of COP31 to secure an overarching agreement was especially significant because it exposed the unresolved status of fossil fuels within international climate diplomacy. The proposed Antalya Pact contained general language supporting the transition towards low greenhouse-gas emissions, renewable energy, and electrification, but it did not explicitly mention coal, oil, or natural gas, nor establish a pathway for transitioning away from them. Instead, it gave considerable prominence to carbon capture, utilisation, and storage as a technological component of the energy transition. The omission became a central objection for the European Union, the United Kingdom, and other countries, while disagreements over climate finance further complicated the negotiations.

The issue was not new. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, governments had agreed to a global effort to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. That language represented an important departure from earlier formulations, which had often referred more generally to emissions reductions and energy efficiency. COP31 offered an opportunity to translate the political commitment into a more concrete implementation pathway. The failure to do so demonstrated how difficult it remains to move from general recognition to specific obligations.

The contradiction is structural. Fossil fuels remain deeply embedded in the global economy, not simply as sources of energy but as foundations of industrial production, transportation, petrochemicals, international trade, employment, public revenue, and geopolitical influence. Countries whose economic structures depend heavily on hydrocarbon production face different transition pressures from those seeking to reduce their dependence on imported energy. Even governments committed to decarbonisation must contend with the immediate requirements of energy security, industrial competitiveness, and employment.

These differences cannot be dismissed as mere excuses. Developing economies such as Bangladesh have legitimate claims to affordable energy, industrialisation, and improved living standards. For countries such as these, constrained access to capital, limited technological capabilities, and inadequate infrastructure, an accelerated energy transition can entail substantial economic and social costs unless it is accompanied by predictable financial assistance, technology transfer, and institutional support. The demand that developing countries undertake an accelerated transition without adequate support risks reproducing the very inequalities that international climate cooperation is supposed to address: those who contributed least to the accumulation of historical emissions are frequently among those with the fewest resources to manage the consequences. 

The influence of fossil-fuel-producing countries adds another dimension. States whose public revenues, investment strategies, and international influence depend heavily on oil and gas have strong incentives to resist commitments that could accelerate the decline of those industries. Their participation in climate negotiations is not inherently illegitimate: they are parties to the international agreement and have a right to defend their economic interests. But the resulting tension between the collective objective of reducing emissions and the individual interests of major producers is difficult to resolve through consensus alone.

The problem extends beyond producing countries. Major consuming economies, including industrialised states, have also maintained substantial dependence on fossil fuels. The transition therefore cannot be understood as a conflict between a small group of oil-producing states and the rest of the international community. It involves a much wider system of production, consumption, finance, infrastructure, and political influence. Because the fossil-fuel economy is deeply embedded in global systems of production, trade, finance, and consumption, its transformation demands more than national commitments or isolated policy interventions. It requires a comprehensive framework of international cooperation underpinned by sustained negotiations and a workable political consensus. 

The Unequal Burden of Climate Responsibility

The politics of fossil fuels cannot be separated from the question of historical responsibility. The climate crisis is global in its consequences, but responsibility for producing it has been distributed unevenly across countries, populations, and generations. Industrialisation in Europe and North America, sustained over more than two centuries by coal, oil, and natural gas, generated enormous wealth while contributing disproportionately to the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Many countries now facing the most severe consequences of climate disruption contributed comparatively little to the historical emissions that produced it.

This asymmetry lies at the heart of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, embedded in the UN climate framework. The principle recognises that all countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but that their obligations cannot be identical when their historical contributions, economic capacities, and developmental circumstances differ so substantially.
Activists hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 20 November 2026, condemning the watered-down negotiating text and highlighting the gap between diplomatic rhetoric and substantive climate action. Photo: Reuters

For developing countries, this is not an abstract diplomatic argument. It concerns the material conditions under which they must pursue economic development while confronting increasingly severe climatic disruptions. Bangladesh, for example, faces the combined pressures of rising sea levels, river erosion, coastal salinity, flooding, cyclones, and the displacement of vulnerable populations. Its exposure to climate risks is disproportionate to its contribution to global emissions. Similar vulnerabilities confront small island states, parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and other regions where limited fiscal resources and inadequate infrastructure constrain the capacity to adapt.

Climate justice therefore requires more than expressions of solidarity. It demands a redistribution of resources, technological capabilities, and adaptation opportunities. Countries that have accumulated wealth through carbon-intensive industrialisation cannot reasonably expect poorer economies to undertake an equally rapid transition without providing substantial financial and technological support. Nor can the international community treat adaptation as an optional supplement to emissions reduction when climatic consequences are already affecting livelihoods, food security, public health, and national infrastructure.

The establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund at COP28 was an important recognition of this problem. It acknowledged that some climate impacts cannot be adequately addressed through mitigation or conventional adaptation measures. Yet the existence of a fund does not resolve the question of its adequacy, accessibility, or predictable replenishment. For vulnerable countries, the difference between an institutional commitment and resources actually reaching affected communities is decisive.

The language of climate justice can also become detached from its material implications. Declarations acknowledging historical responsibility do not necessarily translate into grants, technology transfers, debt relief, or accessible financing. The challenge is not merely to recognise unequal vulnerability but to construct arrangements capable of addressing it.

The Financial Architecture of Broken Promises

Climate finance remains one of the most persistent sources of mistrust in international negotiations. The dispute is not simply about the amount of money required but about who provides it, on what terms, through which institutions, and with what degree of accountability.

Developing countries have repeatedly argued that the financial obligations of wealthier economies cannot be satisfied by announcing ambitious aggregate targets while relying heavily on private investment, loans, and financial instruments that increase the indebtedness of countries already facing severe fiscal constraints. A loan may help finance a renewable-energy project, but it also creates repayment obligations. A private investment may expand electricity generation, but it will generally seek commercial returns. Neither necessarily provides the public resources required to protect communities from flooding, drought, extreme heat, or coastal erosion.

The distinction between grants and loans is therefore fundamental. Countries with limited fiscal capacity cannot be expected to finance adaptation indefinitely through additional borrowing. Nor should climate finance become another channel through which financial institutions impose conditions that restrict domestic policy choices. The provision of climate resources must be evaluated not only by the headline amounts announced but also by their concessionality, accessibility, predictability, and actual delivery.

COP31 exposed this problem once again. Developing countries challenged the proposed adaptation-finance provisions because the proposed tripling of resources lacked a sufficiently clear baseline. The disagreement reflected a wider concern that financial promises could be presented as substantial advances without establishing what additional resources would actually become available.
Local residents work to reinforce a damaged embankment with sandbags, illustrating the frontline realities of community-led adaptation where inadequate finance and infrastructure leave vulnerable populations exposed to recurring disasters. File Photo: Habibur Rahman

There is also a deeper contradiction in the relationship between global financial markets and climate objectives. Capital flows readily towards projects promising measurable returns, but the protection of vulnerable communities often produces benefits that are difficult to monetise. Flood defences, early-warning systems, resilient public infrastructure, agricultural adaptation, and the restoration of ecosystems may generate enormous social value without offering the commercial returns sought by private investors.

Consequently, the mobilisation of private capital, although necessary, cannot substitute for public responsibility. Governments and multilateral institutions must provide the financial foundations for adaptation and ensure that climate investment does not become another mechanism for transferring risk to already vulnerable populations.

The debate also raises questions about international debt. Countries facing recurrent climate disasters may be compelled to borrow for reconstruction, only to encounter further disasters before their previous obligations have been repaid. This creates a cycle in which the consequences of a crisis they contributed relatively little to producing deepen their economic vulnerability. Debt restructuring, disaster-related financing mechanisms, and predictable grant-based support must therefore form part of a credible climate-justice framework.

Consensus as an Instrument of Paralysis

The institutional difficulty exposed at COP31 concerns the relationship between consensus and effective decision-making. The UN climate process derives its legitimacy from the participation of almost the entire international community. Decisions reached through multilateral negotiation carry a political authority that unilateral initiatives cannot easily reproduce. But the same requirement for consensus can make agreement exceptionally difficult when national interests diverge.

At Antalya, the proposed overarching political agreement failed to secure the necessary support. Disagreements over fossil fuels, climate finance, and the treatment of carbon-removal technologies proved impossible to bridge. Although some separate decisions and initiatives advanced, the proposed COP and Paris Agreement cover decisions were not adopted.

This distinction is important. COP31 did not abolish the Paris Agreement, erase previous commitments, or bring international climate cooperation to an end. Its failure concerned the proposed overarching political outcome, not the entire institutional framework. Nevertheless, the inability to agree on the central questions of fossil-fuel transition and financial responsibility reveals the limitations of the existing negotiating architecture.

Consensus serves a legitimate purpose. It protects smaller and less powerful countries from having major decisions imposed upon them by larger economies. It also recognises that climate policies must account for different developmental conditions. A system based exclusively on majority voting could allow powerful coalitions to determine the obligations of countries with very different economic circumstances.

Yet consensus can also become a mechanism of obstruction. When a single government or a small group of governments can prevent agreement on a collective response, the distinction between protecting legitimate national interests and defending the status quo becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. The result may be a diplomatic process in which the language of collective responsibility is repeatedly diluted to accommodate the least ambitious positions.
Activists stage a ‘Kick Big Polluters Out’ demonstration at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 13 November 2026. Photo: Reuters

The problem is therefore not consensus itself but the absence of sufficiently effective mechanisms for translating broad areas of agreement into implementation. A more differentiated approach may be necessary: preserving consensus for fundamental questions of international obligation while allowing willing coalitions to advance specific initiatives on renewable energy, methane reduction, electrification, adaptation, and climate finance.

Such arrangements would not replace the UNFCCC. They could, however, reduce the dependence of practical progress on the successful negotiation of a single comprehensive political declaration. The legitimacy of multilateralism must be preserved, but legitimacy cannot become an alibi for institutional immobility.

The question is how to make international cooperation more consequential without undermining its inclusive character.

The Technological Escape Route

Another difficulty in contemporary climate diplomacy is the growing tendency to frame technological innovation as a possible substitute for politically difficult decisions. Renewable energy, battery storage, electrification, smart grids, and improvements in energy efficiency have transformed the possibilities of decarbonisation. Their expansion is indispensable to any credible climate strategy. But technological optimism can become misleading when it obscures the political and economic choices that determine how technologies are developed, financed, distributed, and deployed.

Carbon capture and storage illustrates this tension. The technology may have a role in reducing emissions from certain industrial processes and addressing residual emissions that are difficult to eliminate. Yet its inclusion in climate agreements raises questions when it is presented as a justification for continued fossil-fuel production. The controversy surrounding the proposed Antalya Pact reflected precisely this concern. Critics argued that an emphasis on carbon-removal technologies could create additional space for fossil-fuel dependence rather than establishing a credible transition pathway.

The issue is not whether carbon capture has any legitimate application. It is whether speculative future technological capacity is being used to defer reductions that are technically and economically achievable today. A strategy that assumes future technological interventions will compensate for continued emissions risks transferring present responsibilities to an uncertain future.

Artificial intelligence introduces another dimension. It can improve climate modelling, assist in predicting extreme weather, optimise electricity grids, monitor deforestation, and support more efficient management of energy systems. These applications may strengthen adaptation and mitigation. Yet the expansion of AI also requires substantial computing infrastructure, electricity, water, semiconductor production, and mineral resources. Its environmental consequences depend on the energy systems and material supply chains that sustain it.

The contradiction is particularly revealing. Technologies developed to improve efficiency may also increase demand for energy and resources. Their net contribution to climate objectives cannot be determined simply by examining their computational or engineering capabilities. It requires an assessment of their entire material and institutional footprint.

The broader point is that technological innovation does not operate outside political economy. The benefits of new technologies are shaped by ownership, access to capital, infrastructure, regulation, and the distribution of economic power. Without appropriate public policy, technological advances may reinforce existing inequalities rather than overcome them.

Climate diplomacy must therefore move beyond the assumption that innovation will eventually resolve contradictions that governments are unwilling to confront. Technology can expand the range of available choices; it cannot make the political choices unnecessary.
A woman stands at the edge of a collapsing riverbank in Harirampur upazila, Manikganj, after losing her fourth home in 30 years to Padma River erosion—underscoring the disproportionate climate impacts borne by vulnerable countries like Bangladesh. Photo: Palash Khan

Beyond the COP Spectacle

The repeated gap between diplomatic declarations and practical outcomes has encouraged a perception that the annual climate conference has become an elaborate exercise in international performance. Thousands of delegates assemble, leaders make announcements, corporations present sustainability commitments, and civil society organisations demand more ambitious action. The conference generates an enormous volume of statements, negotiations, and media attention. Yet the most consequential questions frequently remain unresolved.

The language of spectacle is useful, but it should not obscure the institutional significance of the process. The COP conferences have helped establish climate change as a central concern of international politics. They have created common reporting frameworks, facilitated scientific cooperation, encouraged national commitments, and provided a platform through which vulnerable countries can articulate their demands. The Paris Agreement itself would have been difficult to achieve without sustained multilateral negotiations.

There have also been tangible developments beyond the negotiating texts. The declining cost of renewable energy technologies, the expansion of solar and wind generation, and growing investment in electrification have changed the global energy landscape. These developments cannot be attributed to the COP process alone, but international climate agreements have helped establish policy expectations and investment signals that have contributed to the transition.

Indeed, the international climate regime has not been entirely without consequence. Projections of future warming have improved since the Paris Agreement, although current policies and national commitments remain insufficient to secure the 1.5°C objective. This is an important distinction: the process has helped improve the trajectory without bringing the world close enough to the temperature goal.

The problem, therefore, is not that the COP process has achieved nothing. It is that its achievements remain inadequate relative to the scale and urgency of the crisis. The danger lies in allowing the continuation of negotiations to become evidence of progress in itself. Institutional activity is not equivalent to institutional effectiveness.

A credible reform agenda must begin by making implementation more measurable and accountable. National commitments should be assessed against actual emissions trajectories, energy investment, fossil-fuel subsidies, and the pace of infrastructure transformation. Climate finance should be evaluated by the resources delivered rather than merely announced. Adaptation commitments should be measured by their effects on vulnerable populations, not simply by the creation of new programmes and institutional frameworks.

The relationship between public and private actors also requires closer scrutiny. Corporate participation in climate negotiations can mobilise investment, technical expertise, and innovation. But it can also create conflicts of interest when companies whose revenues depend on carbon-intensive production participate in shaping the language and priorities of climate policy. Transparency about lobbying, financial interests, and the implementation of corporate commitments is essential if the process is to maintain public credibility.

Equally important is the need to strengthen the voice of countries and communities most exposed to climate disruption. The inclusion of vulnerable states in diplomatic negotiations is not merely a matter of procedural fairness. Their experiences provide essential evidence about the practical consequences of inadequate adaptation, insufficient finance, and delayed mitigation. Climate governance cannot be considered legitimate if those bearing the greatest consequences have the least influence over the decisions that determine their future.
Delegates convene at the UN Conference on Environment and Development—the 1992 'Earth Summit'—in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where the UNFCCC was signed to establish a coordinated international response to climate change. Photo: UN

The Limits of Climate Multilateralism

The future of climate diplomacy will depend on whether the international community can move beyond the assumption that increasingly elaborate agreements will eventually produce the necessary transformation. The experience of COP31 suggests that the problem is not simply insufficient ambition but the absence of an institutional arrangement capable of reconciling competing economic interests with the collective requirements of climate stability.

One possibility is to strengthen coalitions of countries willing to advance more ambitious commitments, even when universal agreement remains elusive. Such coalitions could develop common standards for renewable energy, accelerate the phase-out of particularly carbon-intensive technologies, coordinate climate finance, and establish more demanding mechanisms for monitoring implementation. Their initiatives would need to remain compatible with the UNFCCC framework rather than creating competing systems that exclude less powerful countries.

A second priority concerns the relationship between climate obligations and economic policy. Decarbonisation cannot be treated as a separate environmental agenda while trade, industrial investment, energy subsidies, and financial regulation continue to operate according to assumptions that reproduce fossil-fuel dependence. Climate objectives must become integral to economic planning.
