The failure of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), which concluded in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 22, 2026, to secure an overarching agreement exposed once again the widening chasm between the international community's recognition of the climate emergency and its capacity—and political willingness—to respond collectively. After more than two weeks of negotiations, extended beyond their scheduled conclusion, governments failed to agree on an overarching political declaration. The immediate disagreement concerned the omission of any explicit reference to fossil fuels and a pathway for transitioning away from coal, oil, and natural gas. Yet the failure was about considerably more than the wording of a diplomatic document. It revealed the unresolved political and economic contradictions at the heart of international climate governance: governments acknowledge the urgency of decarbonisation while remaining constrained by, and frequently invested in, the very energy systems that sustain global emissions. The question, therefore, is not simply why COP31 failed to reach consensus, but what the recurring inability to translate climate commitments into transformative action tells us about the institutional architecture of global climate diplomacy.

Thirty-one conferences into the process, the annual gathering of governments, diplomats, scientists, corporate representatives, environmental organisations, and civil society has grown into an immense machinery of international negotiation, but its elaborate institutional architecture has done little to overcome the political impasse at the heart of global climate action. The proliferation of these forums reflects a growing recognition that climate change transcends national boundaries and demands coordinated international responses. Yet the multiplication of conferences, declarations, pledges, and implementation frameworks has not produced a commensurate transformation of the global political economy. The gap between diplomatic ambition and material outcomes remains considerable. The irony is difficult to overlook: even as scientific evidence of accelerating climatic disruption becomes increasingly compelling, the negotiations intended to address it remain entangled in competing claims over energy security, economic competitiveness, national sovereignty, historical responsibility, and the distribution of financial burdens.

The question embedded in the title, COP31 Turns into CON31, is deliberately provocative. It asks whether the annual climate conference remains an effective instrument of collective action or has increasingly become a ritual through which governments perform environmental responsibility without having to undertake the political and economic transformations necessary to fulfil their commitments. The distinction is important. To characterize the entire COP process as a con would be to dismiss the genuine achievements of multilateral climate cooperation, not least the Paris Agreement. Yet to regard the continuation of diplomatic negotiations as evidence of meaningful progress would be equally misleading. The more consequential question is whether this institutional process has developed the political capacity to overcome the structural contradictions that repeatedly prevent its declarations and commitments from translating into substantive action.

The Ritual of Climate Diplomacy

The origins of contemporary climate negotiations lie in the 1992 United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which established the principle that climate change required an internationally coordinated response. The annual conferences of the parties subsequently became the principal forum for negotiating commitments, reviewing progress, and developing mechanisms for cooperation. The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 introduced legally binding emissions-reduction targets for developed countries, although its limited participation and uneven implementation exposed the difficulties of reconciling international obligations with national economic interests.

The Paris Agreement of 2015 represented a significant change in approach. Rather than imposing a uniform system of emissions-reduction obligations, it established a framework under which countries would submit nationally determined contributions, periodically strengthen their ambitions, and participate in a collective process of reviewing progress. Its significance lay partly in the recognition that climate action required participation across developed and developing economies. The Paris Agreement established the collective objective of limiting the rise in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while committing its parties to pursuing efforts to restrict the increase to 1.5°C. 

The Paris framework was an important diplomatic achievement. It brought almost the entire international community into a common institutional arrangement and created a mechanism through which national commitments could be progressively strengthened. Yet its architecture also contained a fundamental limitation. The nationally determined character of the commitments preserved considerable discretion for governments, while its transparency and review mechanisms could expose inadequate performance without necessarily compelling corrective action. International cooperation was institutionalised, but the enforcement of national ambition remained limited.

This distinction between agreement and implementation has become central to the COP process. Governments can endorse ambitious temperature targets without agreeing on the domestic measures required to achieve them. They can acknowledge the need for a transition away from fossil fuels while continuing to subsidise, extract, export, and consume them. They can announce financial commitments without establishing sufficiently reliable mechanisms for delivering the resources that vulnerable countries require.

The resulting process is not necessarily fraudulent, nor should the achievements of multilateral climate cooperation be dismissed. Yet institutional legitimacy cannot be equated with substantive effectiveness. International negotiations inevitably involve competing interests, divergent development trajectories, and legitimate disagreements over historical responsibility, economic capacity, and the distribution of adjustment costs. These differences cannot simply be negotiated away. Nevertheless, the repeated production of ambitious declarations without commensurate implementation exposes a fundamental limitation of the process: diplomatic agreement does not necessarily translate into material transformation. A conference may succeed procedurally while leaving the political-economic structures responsible for continued dependence on fossil fuels and unequal exposure to climate risks largely intact. If successive conferences fail to confront these structural contradictions, the question will inevitably arise whether COP32 represents another step towards meaningful collective action or another iteration of COP turning into CON.
COP31 President Murat Kurum (third from left) joins former COP presidents and COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen (fourth from left) in a show of diplomatic unity in Antalya, Türkiye, on 10 November 2026, before negotiations stalled over fossil fuels and climate finance. Photo: Reuters

The Fossil-Fuel Contradiction

The failure of COP31 to secure an overarching agreement was especially significant because it exposed the unresolved status of fossil fuels within international climate diplomacy. The proposed Antalya Pact contained general language supporting the transition towards low greenhouse-gas emissions, renewable energy, and electrification, but it did not explicitly mention coal, oil, or natural gas, nor establish a pathway for transitioning away from them. Instead, it gave considerable prominence to carbon capture, utilisation, and storage as a technological component of the energy transition. The omission became a central objection for the European Union, the United Kingdom, and other countries, while disagreements over climate finance further complicated the negotiations.

The issue was not new. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, governments had agreed to a global effort to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. That language represented an important departure from earlier formulations, which had often referred more generally to emissions reductions and energy efficiency. COP31 offered an opportunity to translate the political commitment into a more concrete implementation pathway. The failure to do so demonstrated how difficult it remains to move from general recognition to specific obligations.

The contradiction is structural. Fossil fuels remain deeply embedded in the global economy, not simply as sources of energy but as foundations of industrial production, transportation, petrochemicals, international trade, employment, public revenue, and geopolitical influence. Countries whose economic structures depend heavily on hydrocarbon production face different transition pressures from those seeking to reduce their dependence on imported energy. Even governments committed to decarbonisation must contend with the immediate requirements of energy security, industrial competitiveness, and employment.

These differences cannot be dismissed as mere excuses. Developing economies such as Bangladesh have legitimate claims to affordable energy, industrialisation, and improved living standards. For countries such as these, constrained access to capital, limited technological capabilities, and inadequate infrastructure, an accelerated energy transition can entail substantial economic and social costs unless it is accompanied by predictable financial assistance, technology transfer, and institutional support. The demand that developing countries undertake an accelerated transition without adequate support risks reproducing the very inequalities that international climate cooperation is supposed to address: those who contributed least to the accumulation of historical emissions are frequently among those with the fewest resources to manage the consequences. 

The influence of fossil-fuel-producing countries adds another dimension. States whose public revenues, investment strategies, and international influence depend heavily on oil and gas have strong incentives to resist commitments that could accelerate the decline of those industries. Their participation in climate negotiations is not inherently illegitimate: they are parties to the international agreement and have a right to defend their economic interests. But the resulting tension between the collective objective of reducing emissions and the individual interests of major producers is difficult to resolve through consensus alone.

The problem extends beyond producing countries. Major consuming economies, including industrialised states, have also maintained substantial dependence on fossil fuels. The transition therefore cannot be understood as a conflict between a small group of oil-producing states and the rest of the international community. It involves a much wider system of production, consumption, finance, infrastructure, and political influence. Because the fossil-fuel economy is deeply embedded in global systems of production, trade, finance, and consumption, its transformation demands more than national commitments or isolated policy interventions. It requires a comprehensive framework of international cooperation underpinned by sustained negotiations and a workable political consensus. 

The Unequal Burden of Climate Responsibility

The politics of fossil fuels cannot be separated from the question of historical responsibility. The climate crisis is global in its consequences, but responsibility for producing it has been distributed unevenly across countries, populations, and generations. Industrialisation in Europe and North America, sustained over more than two centuries by coal, oil, and natural gas, generated enormous wealth while contributing disproportionately to the accumulation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Many countries now facing the most severe consequences of climate disruption contributed comparatively little to the historical emissions that produced it.

This asymmetry lies at the heart of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, embedded in the UN climate framework. The principle recognises that all countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but that their obligations cannot be identical when their historical contributions, economic capacities, and developmental circumstances differ so substantially.
Activists hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 20 November 2026, condemning the watered-down negotiating text and highlighting the gap between diplomatic rhetoric and substantive climate action. Photo: Reuters

For developing countries, this is not an abstract diplomatic argument. It concerns the material conditions under which they must pursue economic development while confronting increasingly severe climatic disruptions. Bangladesh, for example, faces the combined pressures of rising sea levels, river erosion, coastal salinity, flooding, cyclones, and the displacement of vulnerable populations. Its exposure to climate risks is disproportionate to its contribution to global emissions. Similar vulnerabilities confront small island states, parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and other regions where limited fiscal resources and inadequate infrastructure constrain the capacity to adapt.

Climate justice therefore requires more than expressions of solidarity. It demands a redistribution of resources, technological capabilities, and adaptation opportunities. Countries that have accumulated wealth through carbon-intensive industrialisation cannot reasonably expect poorer economies to undertake an equally rapid transition without providing substantial financial and technological support. Nor can the international community treat adaptation as an optional supplement to emissions reduction when climatic consequences are already affecting livelihoods, food security, public health, and national infrastructure.

The establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund at COP28 was an important recognition of this problem. It acknowledged that some climate impacts cannot be adequately addressed through mitigation or conventional adaptation measures. Yet the existence of a fund does not resolve the question of its adequacy, accessibility, or predictable replenishment. For vulnerable countries, the difference between an institutional commitment and resources actually reaching affected communities is decisive.

The language of climate justice can also become detached from its material implications. Declarations acknowledging historical responsibility do not necessarily translate into grants, technology transfers, debt relief, or accessible financing. The challenge is not merely to recognise unequal vulnerability but to construct arrangements capable of addressing it.

The Financial Architecture of Broken Promises

Climate finance remains one of the most persistent sources of mistrust in international negotiations. The dispute is not simply about the amount of money required but about who provides it, on what terms, through which institutions, and with what degree of accountability.

Developing countries have repeatedly argued that the financial obligations of wealthier economies cannot be satisfied by announcing ambitious aggregate targets while relying heavily on private investment, loans, and financial instruments that increase the indebtedness of countries already facing severe fiscal constraints. A loan may help finance a renewable-energy project, but it also creates repayment obligations. A private investment may expand electricity generation, but it will generally seek commercial returns. Neither necessarily provides the public resources required to protect communities from flooding, drought, extreme heat, or coastal erosion.

The distinction between grants and loans is therefore fundamental. Countries with limited fiscal capacity cannot be expected to finance adaptation indefinitely through additional borrowing. Nor should climate finance become another channel through which financial institutions impose conditions that restrict domestic policy choices. The provision of climate resources must be evaluated not only by the headline amounts announced but also by their concessionality, accessibility, predictability, and actual delivery.

COP31 exposed this problem once again. Developing countries challenged the proposed adaptation-finance provisions because the proposed tripling of resources lacked a sufficiently clear baseline. The disagreement reflected a wider concern that financial promises could be presented as substantial advances without establishing what additional resources would actually become available.
Local residents work to reinforce a damaged embankment with sandbags, illustrating the frontline realities of community-led adaptation where inadequate finance and infrastructure leave vulnerable populations exposed to recurring disasters. File Photo: Habibur Rahman

There is also a deeper contradiction in the relationship between global financial markets and climate objectives. Capital flows readily towards projects promising measurable returns, but the protection of vulnerable communities often produces benefits that are difficult to monetise. Flood defences, early-warning systems, resilient public infrastructure, agricultural adaptation, and the restoration of ecosystems may generate enormous social value without offering the commercial returns sought by private investors.

Consequently, the mobilisation of private capital, although necessary, cannot substitute for public responsibility. Governments and multilateral institutions must provide the financial foundations for adaptation and ensure that climate investment does not become another mechanism for transferring risk to already vulnerable populations.

The debate also raises questions about international debt. Countries facing recurrent climate disasters may be compelled to borrow for reconstruction, only to encounter further disasters before their previous obligations have been repaid. This creates a cycle in which the consequences of a crisis they contributed relatively little to producing deepen their economic vulnerability. Debt restructuring, disaster-related financing mechanisms, and predictable grant-based support must therefore form part of a credible climate-justice framework.

Consensus as an Instrument of Paralysis

Another difficulty in contemporary climate diplomacy is the growing tendency to frame technological innovation as a possible substitute for politically difficult decisions. Renewable energy, battery storage, electrification, smart grids, and improvements in energy efficiency have transformed the possibilities of decarbonisation. Their expansion is indispensable to any credible climate strategy. Carbon capture and storage illustrates this tension. The controversy surrounding the proposed Antalya Pact reflected precisely this concern. Critics argued that an emphasis on carbon-removal technologies could create additional space for fossil-fuel dependence rather than establishing a credible transition pathway.

The issue is not whether carbon capture has any legitimate application. It is whether speculative future technological capacity is being used to defer reductions that are technically and economically achievable today. A strategy that assumes future technological interventions will compensate for continued emissions risks transferring present responsibilities to an uncertain future.

Artificial intelligence introduces another dimension. It can improve climate modelling, assist in predicting extreme weather, optimise electricity grids, monitor deforestation, and support more efficient management of energy systems. These applications may strengthen adaptation and mitigation. Yet the expansion of AI also requires substantial computing infrastructure, electricity, water, semiconductor production, and mineral resources. Its environmental consequences depend on the energy systems and material supply chains that sustain it.

The contradiction is particularly revealing. Technologies developed to improve efficiency may also increase demand for energy and resources. Their net contribution to climate objectives cannot be determined simply by examining their computational or engineering capabilities. It requires an assessment of their entire material and institutional footprint.

The broader point is that technological innovation does not operate outside political economy. The benefits of new technologies are shaped by ownership, access to capital, infrastructure, regulation, and the distribution of economic power. Without appropriate public policy, technological advances may reinforce existing inequalities rather than overcome them.

Climate diplomacy must therefore move beyond the assumption that innovation will eventually resolve contradictions that governments are unwilling to confront. Technology can expand the range of available choices; it cannot make the political choices unnecessary.
A woman stands at the edge of a collapsing riverbank in Harirampur upazila, Manikganj, after losing her fourth home in 30 years to Padma River erosion—underscoring the disproportionate climate impacts borne by vulnerable countries like Bangladesh. Photo: Palash Khan

Beyond the COP Spectacle

Thousands of delegates assemble, leaders make announcements, corporations present sustainability commitments, and civil society organisations demand more ambitious action. The Paris Agreement itself would have been difficult to achieve without sustained multilateral negotiations.

Equally important is the need to strengthen the voice of countries and communities most exposed to climate disruption. The inclusion of vulnerable states in diplomatic negotiations is not merely a matter of procedural fairness. Their experiences provide essential evidence about the practical consequences of inadequate adaptation, insufficient finance, and delayed mitigation. Climate governance cannot be considered legitimate if those bearing the greatest consequences have the least influence over the decisions that determine their future.

item.title: The Daily Star – How Sufism and shrine veneration shaped Muslim society in the Bengal delta
item.description:
The process of Islamisation in the Bengal delta was complex, shaped by the region’s pre-existing religious and cultural beliefs and practices. Early Sufis and mystics played a significant role in spreading Islam throughout the region. By establishing khanqahs (Sufi lodges), dargahs (shrines), and mosques, early Sufis helped mediate the relationship between Islamic teachings and the diverse religious and cultural environment. Shrine-centred devotional practices, the veneration of pirs (spiritual masters), and the circulation of vernacular religious literature contributed to the emergence of distinctive forms of Bengali Muslim religious expression.

It has been argued that, even before the establishment of Mughal hegemony, there was scarcely a locality in Bengal without a shrine. A fifteenth-century letter attributed to Mir Sayyid Ashraf Jahangir Simnani (d. 1425), addressed to Sultan Ibrahim Sharqi of Jaunpur (d. 1440?), captures the extent of Sufi influence in Bengal: "In short, in the country of Bengal, what to speak of the cities, there is no town and no village where holy saints did not come and settle down" (quoted in Karim, Social History of the Muslims in Bengal (Down to A. D. 1538), 1985, p. 116). Although this statement should be understood as a representation of the widespread reputation of Sufi saints rather than a literal demographic record, it illustrates the significance attributed to their presence in the region.

The widespread veneration of Sufi saints has frequently led scholars to associate the Islamisation of the Bengal delta with Sufi missionary activity. Yet the historical formation of Muslim society cannot be explained through conversion narratives alone. It involved political transformations, agrarian expansion, settlement patterns, institutional developments, religious encounters, and the production of new forms of religious knowledge. This paper examines these interconnected processes through the historical development of Sufism and shrine-centred religious practices in Bengal. Drawing particularly on the works of Asim Roy, Richard M. Eaton, and Ayesha A. Irani, it argues that Bengali Islam emerged through the interaction of social and geographical transformations, localised religious practices, and vernacular intellectual production.

The geographical territories that constitute the Bengal delta were historically divided into several overlapping regions, including Raṛḥa, Gauṛa, Vanga, Samatata, Harikela, Pundra, and Varendra (Ramesh C. Majumdar, 1971, History of Ancient Bengal; Niharranjan Ray, 1949, Bangalir Itihas: Adi Parbo). Archaeological evidence suggests that Bengal was inhabited from prehistoric times, while its population and cultural formations developed through successive migrations, political expansions, and interactions among indigenous and external communities. 
Devotees carry ceremonial cloths (gilafs) during the annual Urs of Hazrat Shah Jalal in Sylhet, reflecting the enduring significance of Sufi shrine veneration in Bangladesh’s religious and cultural life. Photo: Star

The region experienced several phases of political consolidation before the arrival of Muslim rulers. Chandragupta, the Pala ruler Gopala, and the Sena ruler Vijayasena each contributed to the political integration of parts of Bengal at different historical moments. The conquest of Bengal by Ikhtiyaruddin Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji in 1204 marked the beginning of sustained Muslim political dominance in the region. It also facilitated the movement of Muslim scholars, administrators, merchants, preachers, and wandering dervishes into Bengal. Nevertheless, the expansion of Islam was neither immediate nor uniform. The emergence of Muslim communities was a prolonged process involving political authority, institutional patronage, settlement, agrarian development, and religious interaction.

These interpretations point to an important distinction between formal Islamic institutions and popular devotional practices. The former provided mechanisms for transmitting scriptural knowledge and normative religious teachings, while the latter offered forms of spiritual guidance, intercession, healing, protection, and communal belonging. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

The accommodationist and locally embedded character of Bengali Muslim religious culture encountered sustained criticism during the nineteenth century. Reformist movements sought to redefine Muslim religious identity by challenging practices they considered incompatible with Islamic scriptural norms. Among the most influential were the Fara'idi movement, the Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya, and the Tayyuni movement.

However, the Fara'idi movement cannot be understood exclusively as a campaign for religious purification, even during the leadership of Haji Shariatullah (d. 1840). Under the leadership of his son Dudu Miyan, it developed into a broader peasant mobilisation against oppressive landlordism and colonial agrarian arrangements. Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).

These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

This observation highlights the tension between locally rooted religious practices and movements seeking to establish more standardised forms of Islamic identity.

The subsequent expansion of Deobandi-oriented institutions of Islamic learning, colonial education, and other reformist organisations further transformed the religious landscape. In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.

Drawing on the Arabo-Persian tradition of the Tales of the Prophets (qisas an-nabiya), the work presents Islamic salvation history through Bengali literary conventions and conceptual frameworks familiar to its audience.

Irani demonstrates that the Nabīvaṃśa reflects extensive intellectual and literary exchanges among Muslim, Vaiṣṇava, Nātha, and haṭhayoga traditions. These exchanges reveal common features shared by both Muslim and non-Muslim communities. As Irani observes, they “share a host of these and other common features—theological, narratological, aesthetic, rhetorical, and linguistic—suggests that they participated in overlapping polysystems of performance and reception, of Sufism, Nātha doctrine, haṭhayoga, and Kṛṣṇa bhakti, of orally and textually, evidence of, among other things, the fluency of the circulation of ideas and peoples in the premodern period” (p. 33).

Irani further interprets the Nabīvaṃśa as an example of what she describes as a "Purāṇa-Korān" tradition. In this literary framework, Saiyad Sultan reconstructs prophetic history through a narrative that incorporates pre-Ādamic prophets, Hindu religious figures, and Indic sacred texts into an Islamic account of salvation. The narrative's recurring motif of the earth's appeal for divine intervention provides a framework for connecting different religious histories and establishing Muhammad's prophetic significance (p. 195). It also illustrates the integration of Qurʾānic and purāṇic tropes, highlighting how Sultan appropriated avatāric descent, dharmic genealogy, and the Bangla poetic register to present the prophetic chain.

One of the most significant features of Saiyad Sultan's work is his use of the Vaiṣṇava concept of aṃśāvatāra, or partial divine manifestation, to explain Muhammad's primordial relationship with Allah. Through this conceptual framework, Muhammad is presented in terms intelligible to Bengali readers familiar with Indic theological ideas, while his distinctive status within Islamic prophetic history is maintained (2021, pp. 39–40).

Through the Nabīvaṃśa, Saiyad Sultan attempted to localise Islam by presenting Muhammad in the form of Viṣṇu's kalki avatar in a landscape deeply rooted in the traditions of Gauṛiya Vaiṣṇavism. Thus, Sultan portrayed Islam not as a new religion but rather as the local population's longstanding religious tradition. By integrating Hindu deities and sacred texts into Islamic prophetology, Saiyad Sultan implicitly expands the Qur’anic concept of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) to encompass the Hindu communities of Bengal.

Irani's contribution is particularly important for reconsidering Roy's concept of syncretism. Whereas Roy emphasises the absorption and reinterpretation of local cultural materials within Bengali Islam, Irani directs attention to the literary and theological strategies through which Islamic knowledge was translated into Bengali. The vernacular text did not merely reflect an already established Muslim identity; it actively participated in constructing the intellectual and religious categories through which Bengali Muslims could understand Islamic sacred history. An example of such an attempt is Sultan's use of the term Prabhu Niranjan, rather than Allah, to refer to the Creator.

The difference between the two approaches should not be overstated. Both recognise the importance of Bengali literary production in the historical formation of Muslim religious culture. Their principal difference concerns how the relationship between Islamic textual authority and indigenous cultural forms should be interpreted. Roy foregrounds cultural mediation and syncretistic formation, while Irani emphasises translation, theological articulation, and the vernacularisation of Islamic salvation history.

Regarding the influence of non-Islamic traditions on Sufism, other scholars, in addition to Roy, Eaton, Stewart, and Irani, have argued that it gradually incorporated Tantric, Yogic, Nātha, and other indigenous practices as it developed in the Indian subcontinent.

Muhammad Enamul Haq (1975), in his A History of Sufi-ism in Bengal, for example, suggests that although the fundamental principles of Sufism in Bengal remained comparable to those of northern India until the sixteenth century, Bengali Sufism subsequently developed closer associations with Tantrikism, Yogism, Nāthism, and other similar systems of indigenous thought and asceticism (p. 52). He identifies conceptual parallels between Sufi understandings of the soul, spiritual discipline, and stages of mystical realisation and corresponding ideas in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. His discussion includes comparisons between the Sufi concepts of rūḥ and al-nafs and the Indic concepts of ātman and citta, as well as between Sufi stages of spiritual realisation and Buddhist accounts of spiritual attainment. Such comparisons draw attention to the intellectual encounters that took place between religious communities in the subcontinent. Nevertheless, in assessing the contributions of Sufis in Bengal, Haq acknowledges that Sufis exerted considerable influence on Vaishnavism, particularly on its concept of prema, or divine love, and that the Vaishnava emphasis on a casteless society appeared to derive from Sufi influence. He maintains, “Growth of cordiality and unity between the Hindus and the Muslims of Bengal is one of the great achievements that the Sufis accomplished in this country” (p. 287).

Abdul Karim (1985) also emphasises the institutional and popular dimensions of Sufism in Bengal. He argues that Muslim rulers, in collaboration with Sufi figures, established mosques, madrasas, and khanqahs, which helped introduce local populations to Islamic teachings and institutions. At the popular level, the authority of pirs and the veneration of their dargahs became central features of Bengali Muslim religious life. Karim associates the popular understanding of pir authority with certain familiar aspects of Hindu and Buddhist religious traditions, including the veneration of spiritual teachers and sacred sites. He suggests that such parallels may have facilitated the acceptance of Sufi figures among populations previously familiar with the authority of Tantric gurus and other religious intermediaries. He observes that the Sufis deeply influenced the masses and that, even at the time of his writing, their dargahs or tombs continued to be visited and venerated by both Muslims and Hindus (p. 160).

These interpretations point to an important distinction between formal Islamic institutions and popular devotional practices. The former provided mechanisms for transmitting scriptural knowledge and normative religious teachings, while the latter offered forms of spiritual guidance, intercession, healing, protection, and communal belonging. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

The accommodationist and locally embedded character of Bengali Muslim religious culture encountered sustained criticism during the nineteenth century. Reformist movements sought to redefine Muslim religious identity by challenging practices they considered incompatible with Islamic scriptural norms. Among the most influential were the Fara'idi movement, the Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya, and the Tayyuni movement.

However, the Fara'idi movement cannot be understood exclusively as a campaign for religious purification, even during the leadership of Haji Shariatullah (d. 1840). Under the leadership of his son Dudu Miyan, it developed into a broader peasant mobilisation against oppressive landlordism and colonial agrarian arrangements. Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).
 
Cover of Rafiuddin Ahmed’s The Bengal Muslims 1871–1906: A Quest for Identity (Oxford University Press, 1996, second edition).

The reformist criticism of shrine-centred practices should therefore be situated within a broader transformation of Muslim religious authority. These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (1981, p. 106) characterises an important aspect of nineteenth-century Islamic reform in Bengal as an attempt to reject elements of Bengali cultural life that reformers regarded as incompatible with Islam. This observation highlights the tension between locally rooted religious practices and movements seeking to establish more standardised forms of Islamic identity.

The subsequent expansion of Deobandi-oriented institutions of Islamic learning, colonial education, and other reformist organisations further transformed the religious landscape. In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.

item.title: The Daily Star – Before Plassey: The origins of the East India Company’s land grab in Bengal
item.description:
In late 1698, Charles Eyre, soon to be appointed governor of Fort William in Bengal, persuaded the viceroy, Prince Azim ush Shan, to grant the East India Company a nishan conferring zamindari rights over the three small townships of Sutanuti, Kalkata and Govindpur in exchange for Rs 16,000 and a liberal disbursement of bribes. It was a move later described by Walter Firminger as the most significant and enduring step taken by the Company between 1690 and 1757 (Walter Firminger, Historical Introduction to the Bengal Portion of ‘The Fifth Report’, Cambray, Calcutta, 1917, p. 374). Firminger has to be taken seriously, and so I wish to investigate briefly how the events of 1698 can be situated within the Company’s quest to acquire territory, in the course of which it transformed from a venture concerned principally, but not exclusively, with commerce and trade into a colonising power that came to rule over large parts of the Indian subcontinent (see my Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, on which I have drawn here).

The acquisition of land in India has attracted scholarly interest, but for understandable reasons, the events of the eighteenth century have tended to provide the focus. This was a period, after all, when, following Clive’s victory at Palashi in 1757, the Company acquired territory in Bengal and Bihar on a scale that dwarfed its earlier territorial gains. Compared with the enormity of this land grab, the acquisitions of the seventeenth century were minute, and yet I suspected that in the early decades of the Company, the legal, economic and political foundations were laid for the wholesale plunder that was to follow (see Philip Stern, The Company State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundation of the British Empire in India, Oxford University Press, 2011; and David Veevers, The Origins of the British Empire in Asia, 1600–1750, Cambridge University Press, 2019). 
 
A modern reconstruction shows Sutanuti, Kalikata and Govindpur, the three settlements over which the East India Company acquired zamindari rights in 1698. Map: P. K. Niyogi/Wikimedia Commons.

Indeed, the signs were there from the very start. Hidden amidst the technicalities of the Company's 1600 charter was a clause that empowered it to acquire, retain and dispose of land, not a provision, it has to be said, that we would expect to find in the founding charter of a private, joint-stock company putatively engaged in commerce. The limited power of these seemingly hubristic sentiments, however, was soon exposed by the conditions early factors encountered in India. Not only were they treated with disdain by Mughal authorities, but the futility of the notion that land could be annexed in the face of opposition from an empire with a massive land army soon came to be recognised. Somewhat against the odds, however, the Company was able to lease a commodious house at the great port of Surat, but the factors were only too aware of their vulnerabilities. They could not resist threats to vacate the premises at a moment’s notice, and Mughal officials repeatedly denied them permission to convert the factory into a defensible space by fortifying it.

Frustrated by the intransigence of Mughal authorities and repeated failures to consolidate its position at Surat, the Company turned its attention to the Coromandel Coast on the eastern side of India. Over the ensuing decades, partly through circumstance and partly through political manoeuvring, relatively secure bases were established, most notably in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, which emerged as the three principal sites of the Raj. Our understanding of this process is, however, fragile. What is clear is that early incursions were secured through negotiations between Company agents and indigenous authorities, the details of which cannot be fully grasped without an intimate knowledge of competing systems of land administration and the laws governing land, as well as an appreciation of regional balances of political power.
The cover of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India by John Marriott, published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

Key to this was the relatively small coterie of Company agents who, by forming a branch of subimperialism, effectively conducted affairs in India (see Eric Stokes, The Peasant and the Raj: Studies in Agrarian Society and Peasant Rebellion in Colonial India, Cambridge University Press, 1973). Given that it took six months for a communication from the directors in London to reach India, the agents, legitimately claiming that they knew conditions on the ground best, were able to act autonomously in all spheres of Company endeavour, including the acquisition of land. Under these circumstances, we might have expected some among them to be versed in land law as a precondition for entering into negotiations with indigenous authorities. This, however, was never the case. To the best of my knowledge, no factor was trained in, or indeed possessed even a rudimentary knowledge of, English land law, let alone Mughal or Hindu codes governing the administration of land. The directors were aware of this deficiency and attempted to address it by shipping out small collections of standard legal texts, but it was a futile gesture.

Two urgent questions arise: How did Company agents approach negotiations over land, and to what extent were these conducted within a framework set by English common law? It seems to me that pragmatism, rather than a coherent, unified strategy, held the key to eventual success. In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’
 
An imagined meeting between Robert Clive and Mir Jafar after the Battle of Palashi in 1757. The Company’s later territorial gains dwarfed the small acquisitions of the preceding century. Painting: Francis Hayman, c. 1760; National Portrait Gallery/Wikimedia Commons.

I see agents acting with the same intelligibility as the Company strove to acquire territory in the seventeenth century. When its interests turned to the Coromandel Coast, the site chosen was an unprepossessing fishing village with few natural advantages. The directors initially disapproved of any notion of establishing a settlement, but the agents recognised the potential of Madras, which, crucially, being located in a region beyond Mughal control, would not be subject to the same intransigence experienced in Surat. Indeed, in what was a febrile political climate punctuated by warring factions, the local nayak, Venkatappa, saw in an alliance with the Company an opportunity to boost trade and strengthen his position against rival kingdoms. The kaul subsequently granted in 1638 contained unprecedented concessions, including the right to build a fort and the authority to govern Madras for two years. Because the nayak did not hold alienable rights over the land, however, the Company viewed the arrangement through the lens of common law as a fief under his suzerainty.

This plot, largely infertile and providing, at best, poor foundations for buildings, measured only four square miles, but it was to become the Company's first permanent settlement in India. The initial kaul was renewed, and little time was lost in building what became Fort St George. The security it offered attracted native artisans seeking refuge from the conflicts. They settled outside the walls in their thousands, and the population soared. By 1680, the population of Madras stood at approximately 300,000. In a remarkable missive to the St George council, Josiah Child, the most rapacious of Company chairmen, declared that the place might well provide the foundation of a permanent English dominion in India.
Fort St George at Madras, depicted in an eighteenth-century print. Founded on the Coromandel Coast in the 1630s, the settlement gave the Company a fortified base beyond Mughal control. Source: detail of a print published by J. Fielding in 1782, in John Marriott’s collection.

The next great centre of empire, Bombay, was acquired and grew under very different circumstances. Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.
Two views of the English fort at Bombay, published by Philip Baldaeus in 1672. The Company took control of Bombay in 1668, amid disputes over land held under Portuguese rule. Source: Philip Baldaeus/Wikimedia Commons.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course. 
Job Charnock’s tomb and epitaph in Kolkata. Charnock chose the site of the Company’s future Calcutta settlement. Source: Rangan Datta Wiki/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.
 
A coloured engraving of Fort William in Bengal, belonging to the English East India Company. Printed for John Bowles, it is a reissue of the 1754 original by Jan van Ryne. Image: British Library

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.

Professor John Marriott is a visiting fellow at Kellogg College, University of Oxford, and the author of Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India (Cambridge University Press, 2025).

In a piece mischievously entitled ‘In Defense of Ignorance’, Lauren Benton surveys recent work on the legal politics of the Atlantic world in the early modern period (Lauren Benton, ‘In Defense of Ignorance: Frameworks for Legal Politics in the Atlantic World’, in Brian Owensby and Richard Ross (eds), Negotiating Legal Intelligibility in British, Iberian and Indigenous America, New York University Press, 2018). In legal negotiations with Native American communities, she argues, there was a clear separation on both sides between intelligibility and understanding. The absence of legal training among colonisers did not compromise their position; indigenous legal codes became intelligible to them as agents came to know them through experience and the application of more familiar legal analogies. Put simply, they developed the skills to read the legal landscape and act strategically, often in a shifting political climate, to reach settlements that furthered their interests. ‘Understanding is overrated,’ Benton concludes, ‘both as a legal capacity and as an object of historical inquiry. Abilities to “read” political-legal constraints and to engage in legal practices with even basic competence, in contrast, brought enormous dividends.’

I see agents acting with the same intelligibility as the Company strove to acquire territory in the seventeenth century. When its interests turned to the Coromandel Coast, the site chosen was an unprepossessing fishing village with few natural advantages. The directors initially disapproved of any notion of establishing a settlement, but the agents recognised the potential of Madras, which, crucially, being located in a region beyond Mughal control, would not be subject to the same intransigence experienced in Surat. Indeed, in what was a febrile political climate punctuated by warring factions, the local nayak, Venkatappa, saw in an alliance with the Company an opportunity to boost trade and strengthen his position against rival kingdoms. The kaul subsequently granted in 1638 contained unprecedented concessions, including the right to build a fort and the authority to govern Madras for two years. Because the nayak did not hold alienable rights over the land, however, the Company viewed the arrangement through the lens of common law as a fief under his suzerainty.

This plot, largely infertile and providing, at best, poor foundations for buildings, measured only four square miles, but it was to become the Company's first permanent settlement in India. The initial kaul was renewed, and little time was lost in building what became Fort St George. The security it offered attracted native artisans seeking refuge from the conflicts. They settled outside the walls in their thousands, and the population soared. By 1680, the population of Madras stood at approximately 300,000. In a remarkable missive to the St George council, Josiah Child, the most rapacious of Company chairmen, declared that the place might well provide the foundation of a permanent English dominion in India.
Fort St George at Madras, depicted in an eighteenth-century print. Founded on the Coromandel Coast in the 1630s, the settlement gave the Company a fortified base beyond Mughal control. Source: detail of a print published by J. Fielding in 1782, in John Marriott’s collection.

The next great centre of empire, Bombay, was acquired and grew under very different circumstances. Since 1534, when Sultan Bahadur signed a treaty conferring rights on the Portuguese, the small island and port had languished through neglect and were generally considered to have few prospects. The beleaguered Company at Surat, however, looked to Bombay as a means of opening up trade along the west coast, but the Portuguese resisted any such move. Then, in one of those remarkable events of historical happenstance, Charles II married the Portuguese Infanta Catharina in 1662. As part of the deal, Alfonso ceded control of Bombay, which became Charles's personal demesne, much to the dismay of the Viceroy of Goa, Antonio de Castro, who declared that the treaty would threaten the Portuguese presence in the region, not least by forcing vital legal issues over ownership onto the agenda. While the terms of the treaty were facilitated by shared legal traditions between the English and Portuguese, the practical realities facing Portuguese landowners who risked losing their estates were much less readily resolved, particularly since many were prepared to organise armed resistance.

Charles regarded Bombay as an expensive liability. Quite apart from the turmoil over landownership, there seemed little prospect of it becoming a major trading centre. He offered to sell the island back to the Portuguese crown, but the asking price was exorbitant. Instead, following lobbying, the Company stepped in to take control. And so it was that in 1668, under the terms of a royal charter, all rights, territories and appurtenances were transferred to the Company in return for an annuity of ten pounds. In language that revealed the extent to which the charter was conceived within English codes of common law dating back to the medieval period, Bombay would remain holden to Charles and his successors ‘as the Manor of East Greenwich, in free and common socage, and not in capite, not by knight’s service’ (John Marriott, Land, Law and Empire: The Origins of British Territorial Power in India, Cambridge University Press, 2025, p. 158). In effect, this form of tenure exempted the Company from traditional obligations associated with landholding, including labour and military service.

The Company’s ambitions for Bombay were realised only gradually. Before fortification was completed early in the eighteenth century, the island faced serious problems. The expense of the fort itself, threats from external forces that resulted in its seizure in 1690, land reclamation and even a mutiny that resulted in the capture of the administration for a year all delayed the mission to develop the site as a major trading centre. Against this background emerged a renewed determination to exploit a long-held interest in Bengal. Following a disastrous attempt to capture Chittagong, the chief agent in the region, Job Charnock, sailed up the Ganges in 1690, looking for a suitable permanent site. He chose three small trading villages. At first glance, this pestilential settlement with few trading links was an unlikely option, but situated on the banks of the Ganges, with impenetrable jungle behind it, the site was defensible. Three years later, Charnock died, and so the reputation of this semi-mythical figure as the founder of Calcutta is somewhat misplaced, except that, in retrospect, his initial choice of the site was inspired.

Thus it was that Charles Eyre took over the administration and applied himself to the task of increasing revenue by acquiring land in the immediate vicinity. The three villages soon to become Calcutta were held by a Hindu family as a jaghir, originally granted by Jahangir in recognition of its help in defeating a local maharaja seeking independence. Under Mughal authority, rights to the land, although complicated, would not normally have been transferable to the Company. But events propelled a different course. 
Job Charnock’s tomb and epitaph in Kolkata. Charnock chose the site of the Company’s future Calcutta settlement. Source: Rangan Datta Wiki/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

In 1697, a revolt led by Subha Singh captured Bengal to the west of the Hugli River. The local nawab sought the help of British ships to defeat the rebels, which was agreed to on condition that full tenurial rights over Calcutta be conceded to the Company. These demands were denied; instead, inferior raiyat rights were offered and subsequently accepted, most likely because they included a provision to fortify the new factory. At this point, and with new confidence, Eyre sought to extend his territorial authority. Fully aware that zamindari rights would be resisted by local zamindars, he approached Prince Azim, the Viceroy of Bengal, who acceded to his wishes. Over the ensuing period, Fort William was completed; as in Madras, its protection attracted the settlement of artisans and labourers and attendant increases in revenue, while ever more land came under the control of the Company as zamindar. By 1717, following a concerted campaign of bribery and extortion, the Company received a farman bestowing the right to trade freely in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and to build a factory on any site of its choosing.

In a process more complicated than I have been able to convey in this short account, the East India Company established during the seventeenth century the necessary but not sufficient conditions for the acquisition of large swathes of India. Given the ignorance among factors of even the rudimentary features of English common law governing land, negotiations were likely pursued through corrupt and coercive means, particularly when advantageous opportunities opened up. The language of common law occasionally appeared in the drafting of agreements, but it was little more than window dressing to convey a spurious authority by lending legal legitimacy to arrangements whose practical foundations lay elsewhere.

The Company’s territorial control was confined to small areas around what became the three great presidencies of Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, but the legal, ideological and economic foundations had been laid for the extraordinary land grab of the following centuries. In this respect, land was a vital aspect of Company endeavour. Without land, there was no protection or reliable source of revenue, and ultimately no empire. And yet land also exposed deep fault lines between commerce and conquest, London directors and factors, the Company and rival powers, and between policy and practice. These tensions were not incidental to the Company’s expansion. They were integral to it.

I have been conscious of the multidimensionality of land. If I have tended to focus on the legal and economic dimensions, it is because I lack the detailed knowledge of indigenous traditions of landownership and administration necessary for a detailed investigation of such aspects as identity, belonging and memory. I await with interest to see whether others better versed in indigenous land cultures rise to this challenge.
